THE CHINESE JUNK. The Chinese junk, the Key-Ying, which arrived at New York on the 8th of July, excited there the greatest curiosity. Her light and graceful build, tier sails of matting suspended to her bamboo yards, her smooih and rapid movement þÿ thanks to which, if we may believe the Chinese crew, they have never suffered from had weather þÿ hi short, the singularity of the furniture, which in eludes some dogs with tongues as black as ink, brought by the captain, all combined to attiact a crowd of spectators The prettiest women of New York loved 10 boast of having visited the Chinese junk. Unfortunately the enterprise does not appear to have had the same success in a pecuniary respect. þÿ The Chinese sailors, to the number ol þÿ2( >, not having been pair) their wages, have arrested the vessel, and .Mr. Lord, their advocate, has pleaded for them before the civil court of the district. The crew claim in the first place, their arreais of wages from the month of Seplumber. 1810 ; and in the second, to be sent back to Canton at the expense of the captain. According to the þÿsailors accounts, they were only engaged for eight months, and were not to go beyond Batavia and Singapore The advocate of So Yn Sang Hi, the Chinese captain, replied that the sailors who had worked the ship could not pretend that they had been made to cross the Indian Sea and the Atlantic without their knowledge. With regard to the question of wages, the captain had promised to pay them on their return to

Canton with the produce of the American goods which he was to take on his return. þÿ He added that he did not think the sailors had any right to complain ; the large recompenses they had received fully compensated for what was owed them. The Court derided in favour of the crew, maintained the seizure, ordered the sale of the vessel, and condemned the captain to pay each man one to two hundred dollars, according to rank. Ib.

Phenomena of Light. þÿ Important Discovery. At a late meeting of the Royal Cornwall Polytechnic Society, Mr Hunt addressed the company on the interesting subject of some recent discoveries, and which be himself originated, respecting the various powers of the solar rays. About six years ago, he announced that, associated with the light and heat derived from the sun was another principle, most active in producing extraordinary

a changes in the organic and inorganic world This principle he ai first called Energeia ; hut since, on the suggestion of Sir John Hersnhel, it had been called actinism from the Greek uklin , a ray of the sun. Subsequent researches had established the fact that the solar ray contains thiee principles, and distinct means of action þÿ light, heat, and actinism. His present observations referred to the irifiuence, separately and in combination, of these three principles, on vegetation, showing that seed 4 placed under the influence of solar rays that permeated through yellow glass would not germinate because yellow glass prevents the passage of the actinic principle. with its chemical action. Mr. H. then illustrated by explanations of the various effects on vegetation ol different coloured glasses, the necessity of the combined influence of the three principles of light, treat, and actinism, to the completegermination, growth, and infloiescence of plants. He then showed how beautifully consistent with these recent discoveries were the arrangements of the Divine Being in the process of vegetation. þÿ During spring the solar beam contained a large amount of ihe,actinic principle, necessary at that season tor the germination of seeds and ibe development of birds. In summer tlieie was a larger proportion of the light-giving principle, necessary to the formation of the woody pm lions of plants. And towards autumn, the calorific, or heatgivmg principle, of the solar rays increased.

Mr. Hunt exhibited diagrams showing the proportions ol t he three principles as they had (teen observed to exist in tbe sulur ray, in the seasons of spring, summer, and autumn. He then showed how the vegetation of different climates was variously affected, according as they received different proportions of the three constituent principles of the solar beam. In practical application of the results of his theory, Mr. Hunt spoke of the injurious effects oil vegetation from lire use in greenhouses of the white German sheet glass þÿ Under this kind of glass, plants we re subject to an injurious solar influence which they bad not suffered under the old crown glass. It became, therefore, necessary to discover some means to cut off those paratliermic rays w hich, passing through the white glass, scorched and browned particular portions of the leaves, without culling off the other portions of tfre rays, which weie necessary to the growth of the plant. This remedy Mr. Hum find diseoveied nnd applied at Kew Observatory ; it was a green glass, stained with oxyde copper, of which glass effectually excluded the injutious parathermic rays, while it admitted the oilier solar rays necessary for the plant, as freely as ordinary white glass. In the manufacture of this green glass, it was essential that no manganese should be used, as was the case in while glass. If manganese were used the glass would, after a while, assume a pinkish hue, which would more freely admit the burning rays. Mr.
Hum also spoke of the difference between morning and afternoon rays in their effect on vegetation, and of the probability of vegetation being affected by the polarisation of light þÿ London Paper.

Envelopes þÿ Envelopes to letters are very nice things þÿundoubtedly-, give a letter quite a genteel and fashionable air, þÿ cost nothing more for postage, and eonler a fashionable Character on the writer. Hence in all cases, where an unusual degree of couitesy is intermed, there can be no objection to their employ merit. A letter to a lady, for instance, or to a superior, should always he enveloped. But wlieio the suiject matter of the epistle is business, and where there may possibly be occasion at some lutuie penod to refer to the postmark as a proof ol the time when (be letter wtis mailed, envelopes should be eatefully eschewed. Merchants, therefore, in the transmission of their business correspondence, should never use them. Letters on which the postmaik is not endorsed, (and this is, of coutse, the case, in all letters that are pbt up in envelopes,) ate evidences against the wri ter, but afford none in bis favor

We may brit fly give an instance of this þÿ A shipowner wi ties to an msutance office giving directions to h,»ve bis ship, then tit sea, but of whose Condition he knows nothing, insured. 1 1 is letter is written arm dated on the 5th of the month. On the Htli the' insurance office should have received lire letter, but by some means the letter miscitnies and is not receiv ed until the I3'h, t>ui the instructions of the writer arc obeyed and the vessel is insured. On the iOth the news of the loss of (he

-. . vessel arrives Now the insurance office may refuse to pay the policy, on the ground th&t the order for insurance m this case was written after the owner was aware of the loss. The letter, by miscarriage, of which lite owner knows nothing, certainly did hot arrive until a sufficient lime had elapsed for him to have made use of the information, and the only proof that he did not wute the letter after the 10th would he the post mailt indicating that the letter was mailed on the 5th, his own date on the letter being of coutse no evidence for him. But the envelope has beeu destroyed, and with it the only evidence lie has of his own uprightness in the transaction and the only means he has of substantiating his claims against the underwriters VVe give ibis as a single instance of the inconveniences attending the use of envelopes in tiusiness letters, but many others could be mentioned, had we lime or space. The space of the court yard is open, has a mossaic pavement, and at the walls fantastic pictures of the richest and most tasteful stile. At the sides of the atrium (court-yard) are small sleeping rooms, with the following wall paintþÿjngs: Poli'pheme, who receives a letter ftorn Gulathea, by an amortno riding upon a dolphin; Venus occupied with fishing, a Narcissus, a few swimming gods of Love a Victoria upon a carl, and several land scapes. At the walls of this toom there must have been wood paintings, tbe spaces which they once filled are still plainly seen, as also the charcoal remains of those "paintings. They were, perhaps, fiom the hands of those celebrated masters, Who, according to Pliny, preferred painting upon wood At the side of the reception hall is a dining room, where are seen three large paintings of full size figures. and followed by Bacchant in< s Thirdly, a Bacchanal procession nl tiiuntph with a Victoria. Who engraves into a shield the exploits of the victorious god. Tiie Slave Mother Crossing ttir Ohio. þÿ We remember, says a writer in (he 'Irve Atheiican, the story of n cruel master, who, without cause, had determined to sever a slave mother from her onlv child She had been faithful under the very worst usage, and she determined to remain so, until he told her, that on the morrow her child must lie borne to New Orleans, to he sold there in the shue mart. It was mid-winter. The earth was frosted with a hard crust, yet at midnight she started for the Ohio, determined, if she could, to live and die with her child þÿ She reached its batiks as the putsuers rose the hill beyond ; no boat was near, masses of broken ice were sluggishly drilling along ; what was she to do ? Trusting to Heaten, she put her leei on the treacherous element, and with it bending and breaking beneath her (spectators on either side expecting to see her and her child sink at every moment), she boldly pushed on from cake to cake, until she landed safely on the Ohio shore. Five minutes sooner and she must have perished 5 two minutes later, and she would have met with a winery grave ; for before she had proceeded 20 steps, the ice behind her, close on the Kentucky side, had broken, and was scattered ere she reached the mid river. þÿ " Thank God, you and your child are safe," exclaimed the hard hearted master, as he saw her land, rejoiced that he had escaped the responsibility of their death " Riave-woman." said a Kentuckian, who had witnessed her escape, and met her at the landing, " you
have won your freedom, and shall have it." The mother and child were kept together, and liberty and love are now their lot in their humble but happy home. þÿ «<> +> þÿC:a -

On Imprisonment Ibr Debt. þÿ ooo»- We look with indifference on thq successive parts of human misfortune and affliction, of which if the aggregate were seen together, it would shake ns with emotion. A debtor is dragged to prison, pitidl a moment and forgotten, another follows him and is alike lost in the dungeons of oblivion ; bat when the whole mass of calamity rises up at once, when we think of thousands of human beings groaning in tin necessary misery, not by infirmity of nature, but by the mistaken policy, avarice, or vindictiveness of heartless creditors, who can forbear to pity and lament, to wonder and abhor.

There is no need for declamatory vehemence, we live in an enlightened and philanthropic age, not in the Roman era of heathenism and barbarity, when creditors were allowed to punish their debtors unto death, to dissect, quarter them, and distribute their members among them ;þÿ subsequently mollified to scourging and selling them as slaves, and since modernized into in carceration in a common jail; let us therefore calmly investigate but a few of the manifold evils which imprisonment of debtors brings iqion society. If we consider the relations and effects of consanguinity and the general reciprocation of wants and benefits which make one man dear or necessary to many individuals, it may reasonably l>e supposed that every person languishing in a prison gives trouble of

thus independent of the heaviness of sorrow, impurity of confined air, and want of exercise inflicted on the miserable tenant of a jail, a multiplication of distress is extended in a community. The monastic institutions arc often blamed for having administered to secluded idleness, but whatever ho the evil of such institutions, those have no right t > ceu-ure them whose prisons are o|>en for the infliction of worse evils on unfortunate debtors, whose jails are crowded with sufferers, oftentimes hardened and depraved by long confinement, despair, want of occupiti m and lied associations. It is surely less criminal to p rtuit Ihau to compel inaction, to allow mistaken rotir uent than to enforce depraving seclusion : and what ii worc is that tliis rigour of the law generally Hills on the most innocent and the most deserving of com nisserition. whilst the unfair debtor, those who have meditated their fraud, are always those who are toe least susceptible of the sufferings the others in a g reater degree undergo from consciousness of not having merited them.

It is hut too common a motive with creditors, to throw their unfortunate tellow creatures in'oa jail with a view of compiling some w orthy relative or friend to liquidate the debt. Is tins conscientious, fair, or moral ? I will reimburse myself, I (taro not hv what amount of injustice, at what expense of principle. nr if I even extract it from the better feelings of one who does not owe me.

I have arrested him (says another) not that I expect any benefit from it, but because it will punish him, and I will at least have that satisfaction. In many cases no doubt they have real, or apparent cause from some circumstances connected with the incurrence of the debt ; but, an eye for un eye, and a tooth for a tooth, is not a Christian maxim. It is useless to sophisticate ; Christianity is untrue, or it is imperative. Forgiveness of injury is its precept, its command, and must therefore lie its þÿdisciple s practice. Besides, the law which never was intended to gratify useless private revenge, might surely here, without injustice, interpose as much to the benefit of the credo' or u the debtor, and limit the duration of coniinernen:. wmcli, the former blinded by anger, would exvnd to an unreasonable time, though each day lessons his prospect of payment by increasing the disability of Ills prisoner.

Surely In' whose debtor perished in prison, though he may acquit himself of intentional murder, must at least have his mind clouded with douls as to the unrelentingnoss of his nature, and the extent, of his guilt if there be any so olxlurate by avarice, so caiious to humanity as to revolve these various consequences without dread or pity, I must leave them to lie awakened by some other power, for I write only t > Christian hearts and hr. man beings, and such a> are neither, w ill I hope ere long, lie deprived by onr legislators, of the power of offering up human victims to their golden idol VERUS. Another Account from the (liold Region- Brewer, Feb. 1, 1849 Editor of the Bangor Whig:-- The interest felt in anything pertaining to the gold region, induces me to place at vour disposal the following extract of a letter received this morning, from my brother at the Sandwich Islands. The extract is composed chiefly of an extract of a letter from a gentleman who had been on the ground two months. Yours, truly, Nathan Dole. Punahon. Nov. 2, 1848. I received a letter last week from , dated Oct. 2d. He writes þÿ active diggings are now going on over a tract more than 200 miles in length by 10 to 40 in widih ; 5.000 or 0,000 are probably mining, and at least $2,000,000 have been drawn from this bank, since it commenced specie payment, six months ago. A þÿday s work ranges from nothing up to a thousand dollars þÿ hut of those who labor steadily, the average daily income ts probably not far from an ounce. The gold is found in the stratum called by geologists diluvium or drift, composed of loose pebbles, sand, and gravel, and occurs most abundantly in tire bottom of dry ravines, where it lies from a lew inches to three or four teet below the surface When a new ravine is discovered in what are called the ' dry diggings." there is an immediate rush for it. and it becomes Idled with active diggers, each claiming a portion, from a lew feel to a few yards m length ; and a ditch is soon dug two or three feet nr more in width, and down to the rock on which the stratum of drift rests. This ditch is excavated in a few days, and if the

ravine is of ordinary richness, will yield from $500 $1,000 or $5,000 for every rod in length þÿ much of it in lumps large enough to be picked out without washing þÿ some of them of the size of þÿpullet e s ggs or larger. My brother adds þÿ One might suppose, from reading r tic above, that digging gold is very piotilable business, but there are other tilings to be considered At San Francisco hnuid and lodging, three in a tied, or on the floor, is from $20 to $110 a week. Fork is $50 a barrel, and butter $1 a þÿ pound, at wholesale. At the mines pork is $200 a barrel. And then the sickness Nine tenths of all who have gone to the mines have been taken sick. Hundreds were lying sick at Suiter's Fort, unable to procure a passage to S iu Francisco, and suflering from want of attendance and of the necessaries ol life. þÿ Bilious and intermittent fevers prevail to an alarming extent Take all things into ac count, and I think those that stay at home the best off. Mv correspondent says that t hero is vastly less quarrelling than he h id anticipated, hut there is drinking and gambling. and all are on a level at the mines." þÿ Mr. H. has gone to San Francisco, to see what he can do to persuade i he people to lay up a treasure in heaven lie will doubtless find full employment among the sick and riving. Two individuals who went from Honolulu have been murdered þÿ one of them leaving a wife, a very excellent woman, and four or five children. He hud been addicted to di inking and gambling.
still further discoveries. Information has reached tins city of a new dis -overv of gold regions hi the vicinity ol

From the Washington Union of Wednesday. 1 lito re 4 i n g þÿf ruiii þÿI nsiumu. We have been furnished with tire following extracts from a letter written by General P F. Smith, at Panama, datsd the 7th January. and lay them before our readers, as containing mailers <d importance, especially to that portion of our fellow citizens wtio are preparing to visit California. Panama, January 7. 18 19 The situation of affairs hi California is really most extraordinary No accounts we had aie exaggerated. Capi. Henrian de 1. angle, ol the French brig <d war Genin, now here, savs that he learned at Valparaiso and Lima, that there laid been brought to those places Irom Calilornia, to be run into tiars, gold to the amount of nine millions ol francs (near $1,800,000 ) The British consul tells me he has forwarded 15 000 ounces Irom this place across the isthmus; and Lieutenant Wood, of the Braiisti navy, commanding Ihe Pandora, now here, says that the troth is beyond the accounts we have heard. These gentlemen also sav that hundreds of people Irom the western coast of South \merica are embarking for the gold region: and most of lire c.lei ks in the commercial places have quit their employments tor the same object. It will evidently he impossible to prevent the troops, when they arrive, from deserting, and there will he no force to control the crowd of adventurers that will arrive. #

No preparation was made here by the steamboat company tor transporting passengers across ihe Isthmus, or affording them any information or aid in relation to it. The roads are almost impassable even |<>r mules, and the number ol boats on the river and animals on the roads, is entirely insufficient. The public property in charge of the qoartermusieis has tieen L ing a week at Cruces, wailing for þÿ .it)or 40 mules to carry it ; and the trouble, vexation and exposure in gelling il up t fie river Ghagres to (Ins place, brought on Captain Elliot, the senior qnaitermaster, an attack of cholera, of which lie died, on the night ol ihe 5<h; and was buried the nt xt day at Cruces, in lire church yard. Major Frz 'er.ald has taken charge of the property : bin lie is now ruck here of a similar attack I have directed all the public propei i v and office's' baggage now there to lie brought at once to this place, which is more healthy. The greater paM of it will fie carried on þÿmen h s acks. Tl.ec are now usking $20 a piece for mule loads of one-

third of the ordinary weighi, the usual price being from $4 to $5 for full loads. 1 will not attempt to describe t tie roads, or paths Under these circumstances, I think it will not be wise to send anything by tins route except a messenger with a very small trunk, until other arrangements aie made. The resources of the isthmus are entirely unequal to the business now thronging to it. Flour is to day at $40 a barrel : and the inhabitants of the town are alarmed at the prospect ot pestilence and famine. þÿ Mr. Birch, a very fine young man, a mechanic from Washington, is one of tiie victims of the cholera at Cruces.
